name: Half Guard to Kimura Trap
summary: Half Guard to Kimura Trap is a bottom-side control entry that threads the inside arm under the opponent's exposed tricep to lock a figure-four grip, converting half guard retention into the Kimura Trap control system.
description: Learn Half Guard to Kimura Trap in BJJ. Thread the inside arm, lock the figure-four grip, and enter the Kimura Trap control system from half guard bottom.
overview:
Half Guard to Kimura Trap is the control entry that connects half guard bottom to the Kimura Trap system. It is a positional entry, not a finish: the success outcome establishes the figure-four grip and the control structure that comes with it, and the submission is a separate decision taken from there. That distinction is the whole point of the node. A move whose success edge reaches the game-over sink is a submission and is authored as one; this move's success edge reaches a position, so it is a transition.

The entry opens when the top player commits their arm — posting a hand on the mat to base, reaching across for a crossface, or driving an underhook deep during a pass attempt. The bottom player, on their side with the inside hip elevated, threads their inside arm under the exposed tricep, grips their own wrist, and closes the figure four. The half guard leg entanglement is what makes the grip matter: it anchors the top player in place while the shoulder is isolated, so they cannot simply stand up and pull the arm free.

Once the grip closes, the position inverts. The Kimura grip controls the opponent's shoulder girdle regardless of who is nominally on top, which is why the Kimura Trap is authored as a control system rather than a submission setup. From there the bottom player's options fan out into sweeps, back takes and the finish itself. Failing the entry usually costs nothing but the grip — you are still in half guard — which is why it is a low-risk, repeatable attack. Losing it badly means the top player clears the entangled leg while your arm is committed, and you concede the pass.
conditions: Top player's arm is exposed — posted on the mat for base, reaching for a crossface or underhook, or extended during a pass attempt
Bottom player is on their side with the inside hip elevated, not flattened on their back
The half guard leg entanglement is intact and anchoring the top player's near leg
Enough space exists between the two chests to thread the inside arm under the opponent's tricep

variants_and_adaptations.description: Establish the lockdown on the trapped leg first to break the top player's posture and stall their pass, then attack the posted arm as they re-base. The lockdown removes their ability to disengage while the grip is being built.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Against a heavy, posture-strong top player who will not give up the arm until their base is threatened.

variants_and_adaptations.description: From a knee shield half guard, use the shield to hold distance and bait the crossface. When the top player reaches over the shield to flatten you, the reaching arm is already extended and the figure four closes on it directly.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When you are playing a distance-based half guard and the opponent's pass attempt starts with an upper-body reach.

position_integration: This is the gateway node between half guard bottom offense and the Kimura Trap control system, and it is the only success-result arrival into Kimura Trap/Bottom. Without it, that state is enterable only by failing one of your own moves, which makes an entire authored control system reachable by accident and never on purpose. It sits alongside the other Half Guard/Bottom control entries — Half Guard to X-Guard, Half Guard to K-Guard, Half Guard to Old School — as an alternative offensive line when the underhook sweeps and back takes are being defended, and it feeds the Old School Sweep, Kimura Sweep and Half Guard to Back Take lines that Kimura Trap/Bottom deals.

attacker.name: Half Guard to Kimura Trap — Attacker
attacker.description: The bottom half guard player threading the inside arm to close a figure-four grip and enter the Kimura Trap.
attacker.overview: As the attacker you are on the bottom of half guard, and your job is to trade a moment of arm commitment for a grip that outlasts the position. Stay on your side with the inside hip off the mat: flat on your back the thread has no room and your shoulder has no leverage. Wait for the arm — do not chase it. The top player will post to base, reach for the crossface, or extend during a pass, and any of the three exposes the tricep. Thread, grip your own wrist, and close the figure four before you think about where you are going with it. The grip is the position; everything after is a choice.
key_principles: The grip is the objective — do not trade it for a sweep or a finish before it is closed and deep
Stay on your side with the inside hip elevated; a flattened hip removes both the thread space and the shoulder leverage
Take the arm the opponent gives you rather than hunting a specific one — post, crossface and underhook all expose the tricep
Keep the half guard leg entanglement live throughout; the grip only controls because the legs prevent disengagement
Close the figure four as close to the opponent's elbow as the arm allows — a wrist-end grip gives the shoulder room to rotate free
Treat a failed entry as free: you return to half guard having spent only grip effort, so the attack is repeatable
setup_requirements: Half guard established with the opponent's near leg entangled and controlled
Bottom player on their side, inside hip elevated, head off the mat
The opponent's near arm posted, reaching, or otherwise extended away from their ribs
Free hand available to meet the threading arm and close the figure four

execution_steps.description: Shrimp onto your inside hip so your shoulders are stacked vertically rather than flat. This creates the gap under the opponent's chest that the threading arm needs and puts your shoulder in a position to generate rotation.

Confirm the half guard entanglement on the opponent's near leg, adding the lockdown if their base is strong. The legs are what convert a grip into control by removing the option to stand and pull free.

execution_steps.action: Wait for the arm to commit
execution_steps.description: Let the opponent post to base, reach for the crossface, or drive an underhook. Do not reach for an arm that is still tight to their ribs — a premature thread gives them your back and costs you the underhook battle.

Drive your inside arm under the exposed tricep and up along the far side of their arm, palm turning toward their back. Keep the elbow tight to your own body as it travels so the arm does not get flattened out.
Meet the threading hand with your free hand, grip your own wrist, and close the loop over the top of their arm. Slide the whole grip toward their elbow to shorten the lever they can rotate against.

Pull the captured arm across their centreline or toward their back to load the shoulder, and re-settle your hips underneath. You are now in Kimura Trap Bottom with the grip established and the finish, the sweep and the back take all available as separate decisions.

common_counters.counter: Hiding the arm — the top player keeps the elbow pinned to their ribs and refuses to post
common_counters.your_response: Attack their base instead: lockdown or off-balance them so they must post to stay upright, then take the arm they are forced to give.

common_counters.counter: Ripping the arm free before the figure four closes
common_counters.your_response: Close the loop earlier and higher on the arm, and keep your threading elbow tight so there is no straight line for them to extract along.

common_counters.counter: Passing the entangled leg while your arm is committed
common_counters.your_response: Abandon the thread the moment the leg is cleared and recover the knee shield; the grip is not worth the pass.

common_errors.consequence: No space under the opponent's chest and no shoulder leverage, so the arm gets pinned and the underhook is lost.
common_errors.correction: Shrimp onto the inside hip first and confirm your shoulders are stacked before the arm moves.

common_errors.error: Reaching for an arm that has not committed
common_errors.consequence: The opponent circles the arm free and takes the underhook you vacated, often ending in a pass.
common_errors.correction: Bait the commitment with a lockdown or an off-balance and take the arm only once it is posted or extended.

common_errors.error: Gripping at the wrist end of the arm
common_errors.consequence: The lever is long, the shoulder rotates free easily, and the trap never consolidates.
common_errors.correction: Walk the closed figure four toward the elbow before you load the shoulder.

common_errors.error: Releasing the leg entanglement to chase the grip
common_errors.consequence: The opponent stands or steps over, and the grip controls nothing because they can disengage.
common_errors.correction: Treat the legs as a prerequisite, not an afterthought — the entanglement stays live for the whole entry.

common_errors.error: Going straight for the finish as the grip closes
common_errors.consequence: You surrender the positional consolidation and the opponent extracts during the rotation.
common_errors.correction: Establish the trap first. The finish is a separate decision made from an established position.

training_progressions.description: Partner posts a hand on the mat and holds still. Thread and close the figure four for reps until the path is automatic from both the knee shield and the flat half guard.
Partner passes at 50% and may post, crossface or underhook. Take only the arm that commits; reset without threading if none does.
Partner actively hides the arm and defends the loop. Start in half guard bottom, win the grip or reset after thirty seconds.
From live half guard bottom rolling, enter the trap and consolidate only — no finish, no sweep — to train the positional discipline the entry depends on.

flashcards.question: Why is Half Guard to Kimura Trap authored as a transition rather than a submission?
flashcards.answer: Because its success outcome establishes a position — Kimura Trap/Bottom — rather than reaching the game-over sink. A move whose success edge reaches game-over is a submission and is authored as one; this one's success edge reaches a position, so it is a transition.
flashcards.answer_line: Success edge lands on a position

flashcards.question: What must be true about your hips before you thread the arm?
flashcards.answer: You must be on your side with the inside hip elevated and your shoulders stacked vertically. From a flat back there is no gap under the opponent's chest to thread through and no shoulder leverage to rotate with.
flashcards.answer_line: On your side, inside hip elevated

flashcards.question: Which three opponent actions expose the arm for this entry?
flashcards.answer: Posting a hand on the mat to base, reaching across for the crossface, and driving an underhook deep during a pass attempt. All three extend the arm away from the ribs and expose the tricep to the thread.

flashcards.question: Why does the half guard leg entanglement have to stay live during the entry?
flashcards.answer: The grip only converts into control because the legs stop the opponent standing up or stepping away to pull the arm free. Release the entanglement and you hold a grip on someone who can simply disengage from it.

flashcards.question: Where on the arm should the closed figure four sit, and why?
flashcards.answer: As close to the opponent's elbow as the arm allows. A grip at the wrist end leaves a long lever that the shoulder can rotate free against, so the trap never consolidates.
flashcards.answer_line: Toward the elbow, not the wrist

flashcards.question: What is the cost of a failed entry, and what does that imply?
flashcards.answer: You return to half guard bottom having spent only grip effort, so the attack is low-risk and repeatable. The real cost only appears if you keep the arm committed while the opponent clears the entangled leg, which concedes the pass.

attacker.safety_considerations: This is a control entry, not a submission, and no joint should be loaded during it. Closing the figure four captures the shoulder but must not rotate it: the finish is a separate, deliberate decision made from the established trap. Threading fast into a partner's committed arm can hyperextend an elbow that is already straight, so build the grip progressively and never snap it closed.

defender.name: Half Guard to Kimura Trap — Defender
defender.description: The top half guard player denying the arm and preventing the figure-four grip from closing.
defender.overview: As the top player your defence is decided before the grip closes, not after. Once the figure four is locked and consolidated you are in their control system and every option costs you something. The whole defensive game is therefore about arm discipline: base without posting your hand where it can be threaded, crossface without extending, and pass without feeding the underhook arm. If the thread starts, your window is the moment before the two hands meet — that is when the arm still comes out cleanly. After that, your best line is usually to accept the grip and pass the entangled leg rather than fight the shoulder.
key_principles: Win this before the grip closes — after the figure four consolidates every option costs you something
Base on your head, knee and hip rather than a posted hand whenever the bottom player is on their side
Keep the elbow pinned to your ribs; an arm tight to the body has no tricep gap to thread under
If the thread starts, extract before the two hands meet — that is the only clean window
Once the grip is closed, pass the entangled leg instead of fighting the shoulder — position beats grip strength
Never let them flatten you onto your side while the grip is live; that is the sweep, not the submission
recognition_cues: The bottom player shrimps onto their inside hip and their shoulders stack vertically
Their inside hand starts travelling under your near tricep rather than framing on your hip
They stop attacking the underhook and go quiet, waiting for your arm to commit
The lockdown closes on your trapped leg, which usually precedes an attack on your base

defensive_options.action: Hide the arm — keep the elbow pinned to your ribs and base on head, knee and hip
defensive_options.when_to_use: Pre-emptively, whenever the bottom player is on their side with an elevated hip.
defensive_options.if_successful: The entry never starts and you continue your pass.
defensive_options.risk: Basing without a posted hand is less stable; a committed off-balance can sweep you.

defensive_options.action: Extract early — rip the arm straight back before the two hands meet
defensive_options.when_to_use: The instant you feel the thread begin and the loop is still open.
defensive_options.if_successful: You recover the arm and are back to a neutral half guard pass.
defensive_options.risk: Ripping late feeds the grip and can load your own shoulder.

defensive_options.action: Concede the grip and pass the leg
defensive_options.when_to_use: The figure four is already closed and consolidating.
defensive_options.if_successful: You reach side control with the arm still gripped but the entanglement gone, which neutralises the trap.
defensive_options.risk: Committing to the pass while the shoulder is loaded exposes you to the finish and the back take.

favorable_outcomes.how: Clear the trapped leg with a knee cut or a back step the moment their inside arm leaves its frame, then drive to side control before the figure four consolidates. This is the counter outcome: you pass while their arm is committed to the thread.
Extract the arm before the loop closes and re-establish your base. The entry fails, nothing changes, and you return to the same half guard pass you started.

common_errors.error: Posting a flat hand on the mat to base
common_errors.consequence: You hand over the exact arm the entry needs, fully extended, with the tricep exposed.
common_errors.correction: Base on head, knee and hip instead, and post only on the far side away from the thread.

common_errors.error: Fighting the shoulder after the grip is closed
common_errors.consequence: You spend energy against a lever designed to beat arm strength, and lose the passing window.
common_errors.correction: Accept the grip and change the problem — pass the entangled leg and the trap loses its anchor.

common_errors.error: Ripping the arm late, after the two hands have met
common_errors.consequence: The rotation loads your own shoulder against the closed figure four and can finish you.
common_errors.correction: Extract only while the loop is open; once it is closed, switch to the positional answer.

common_errors.error: Reaching across for the crossface against an elevated hip
common_errors.consequence: The reaching arm is the most commonly captured one in this entry.
common_errors.correction: Flatten their hip first, then crossface — never crossface into a bottom player who is already on their side.

flashcards.question: When is the defensive window for this entry, and why does it close?
flashcards.answer: The window is the moment before the bottom player's two hands meet. Once the figure four closes and consolidates you are inside their control system, and every remaining option costs you either the position or the arm.

flashcards.question: Why is basing on a posted hand a mistake here?
flashcards.answer: A posted hand is a fully extended arm with the tricep exposed, which is precisely what the thread needs. Basing on head, knee and hip keeps the elbow pinned to the ribs and leaves no gap to thread under.
flashcards.answer_line: A posted hand is the arm they want

flashcards.question: Once the figure-four grip is closed, what is the better answer — the shoulder or the leg?
flashcards.answer: The leg. Fighting the closed grip pits arm strength against a lever built to beat it, while passing the entangled leg removes the anchor that makes the grip into control, and it takes you to side control.
flashcards.answer_line: Pass the leg, not the shoulder

flashcards.question: What is the danger of ripping the arm out late?
flashcards.answer: Pulling straight back against an already-closed figure four rotates your own shoulder against the lock, which can finish you rather than free you. Extract only while the loop is still open.
flashcards.answer_line: It rotates you into the lock

training_progressions.description: Hold half guard top against a partner on their side for one-minute rounds without posting a hand on the mat. Base on head, knee and hip only.
Partner threads slowly and announces the moment their hands meet. Practise extracting before that call, then practise recognising when it has passed.
Start with the grip already closed. Your only objective is to pass the entangled leg to side control without fighting the shoulder.
